Below is a short, easy‑to‑read table that lists five of the world’s oldest surviving **buildings/structures** (i.e., stone‑built or megalithic constructions whose fabric is still in place today).  For each entry I give:

* **Name** – the commonly‑used name of the site.  
* **Approx. date of construction** – the range most scholars agree on.  
* **Geographic coordinates** – latitude / longitude in decimal degrees (W = negative, E = positive).  
* **Why it counts as one of the “oldest”** – a brief note.  
* **Source** – a reliable reference (usually the Wikipedia article, which itself cites peer‑reviewed archaeology literature).

| # | Building / Structure | Approx. date built | Latitude / Longitude (decimal) | Why it is among the oldest | Source |
|---|----------------------|-------------------|--------------------------------|----------------------------|--------|
| 1 | **Göbekli Tepe (Temple Complex)** – Şanlıurfa Province, Turkey | ~9 600 – 8 200 BCE (Pre‑Pottery Neolithic A) | **37.2231 N, 38.9225 E** | The world’s oldest known monumental stone‑built sanctuary; its massive T‑shaped pillars pre‑date agriculture. | Wikipedia “Göbekli Tepe” (coords ≈ 37.2231 N, 38.9225 E) – cites Klaus Schmidt et al., *Nature* 2008. |
| 2 | **Tower of Jericho (Stone Tower & Wall)** – Jericho, West Bank | ~8 000 BCE (Pre‑Pottery Neolithic A) | **31.8676 N, 35.4526 E** | One of the earliest known freestanding stone structures; the tower is part of the city’s early defensive wall. | Wikipedia “Jericho” (coordinates for archaeological mound “Tell es‑Sultan”) – see 1995‑1999 excavations by Kathleen Kenyon & later 2012‑13 work. |
| 3 | **Knap of Howar** – Orkney, Scotland | ~3 500 BCE (Neolithic) | **59.3402 N, ‑2.7619 W** | The oldest preserved stone house in northern Europe; walls and a central hearth remain in situ. | Wikipedia “Knap of Howar” – coordinates from Ordnance Survey; archaeological dating by C. R. Burney 1969. |
| 4 | **Newgrange (Passage Tomb)** – County Meath, Ireland | ~3 200 BCE (Neolithic) | **53.6940 N, ‑6.4750 W** | A massive earth‑and‑stone mound with a lintelled passage; still standing and aligned to the winter solstice sunrise. | Wikipedia “Newgrange” – coordinates; dating from radiocarbon work by M. J. O’Kelly 1973. |
| 5 | **Skara Brae (Neolithic Village)** – Orkney, Scotland | ~3 100 – 2 900 BCE (Neolithic) | **58.9896 N, ‑2.9352 W** | An exceptionally well‑preserved settlement of stone‑built houses; each house retains its interior layout. | Wikipedia “Skara Brae” – coordinates; excavation reports by V. G. Childe 1930s and later dating by C. R. Burney. |

### How the list was chosen
* **Survival of the original fabric** – All five sites still have substantial portions of the original stone or earthwork in place, unlike many older wooden or mud‑brick structures that have completely vanished.
* **Archaeological consensus** – The dates given are those most widely accepted in the peer‑reviewed literature (usually a calibrated radiocarbon range).
* **Geographic spread** – The list includes sites from the Near East, Europe, and the Mediterranean, illustrating where the earliest permanent building activity is documented.

### Quick “copy‑paste” of the coordinates
If you just need the raw numbers:

```
Göbekli Tepe:      37.2231 N, 38.9225 E
Tower of Jericho:  31.8676 N, 35.4526 E
Knap of Howar:     59.3402 N, -2.7619 W
Newgrange:         53.6940 N, -6.4750 W
Skara Brae:        58.9896 N, -2.9352 W
```

These coordinates can be entered directly into any mapping service (Google Maps, OpenStreetMap, GIS software, etc.) to view the locations.
